title: Subspace Inference Enables Efficient Active Reward Learning from Preferences
abstract: Reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) has emerged as a powerful yet sample-inefficient approach for learning reward models from human preferences, making active learning a critical component in synthesizing informative preference queries. However, effective uncertainty quantification required for active learning remains a key challenge for large neural network reward models. In this paper, we introduce PreferenceEKF, a sample-efficient approach that tracks reward model uncertainty by framing active preference learning as a sequential Bayesian filtering problem. Instead of relying on computationally prohibitive posterior inference over the full neural network parameter space, our method performs sequential inference via an extended Kalman filter within a low-dimensional parameter subspace, continuously updating the reward model posterior as new preference queries arrive. Our approach enables scalable sampling of neural network parameters to efficiently compute acquisition functions for active reward learning. Experiments on the D4RL and V-D4RL benchmarks demonstrate that our approach achieves better sample efficiency, runtime, scalability, and calibration compared to other Bayesian deep learning approaches, and the learned reward models lead to competitive offline reinforcement learning policy performance. This highlights the potential of scalable Bayesian methods for preference-based reward modeling in RLHF. Our code is available at https://github.com/yutaizhou/bnn_pref.

title: Symmetries and Causality: Causal Effect Identification Beyond IID Data
abstract: In the natural sciences, symmetries and cause-effect relationships are ubiquitous. Yet for complex machine-learning tasks, like world-modeling in reinforcement learning, they appear difficult to harness. We propose a formal description of statistical systems based on symmetries in data leaving causal mechanisms invariant. The result is an abstract, simple and general mathematical language for causal reasoning. This paper provides formal descriptions of models and queries, setting up this language, and the formal infrastructure and strategies for their mathematically rigorous identification from data within this formalism. This approach reproduces and matches standard theoretical results on IID data and transport of experimental and non-experimental data. But its main purpose is to unify and substantially extend the scope of causal reasoning, in going beyond IID data and in approaching complex causal queries not captured by do- or soft-interventions. This new perspective on causally relevant aspects of data-modeling additionally sheds new light on well-known structures like c-components or hedges but also includes aspects of missing data and is inherently well-suited for the description of transfer and robustness properties.

title: When Models Edit Too Much: On the Fidelity of Minimal Code Edits
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to edit existing code, but correctness alone is not enough: useful repairs should also be minimal, reviewable, and faithful to the original implementation. We study over-editing, the tendency of a model to rewrite code beyond what is required to fix a bug. We construct an evaluation framework from 400 BigCodeBench problems by injecting controlled AST-level corruptions into reference solutions, giving each repair task a known minimal patch. Across frontier LLMs, over-editing is widespread even among strong models like GPT-5.5: high Pass@1 can coexist with unnecessarily large edits and added cognitive complexity. A preservation instruction substantially reduces this behavior, lowering average excess Levenshtein distance from 0.195 to 0.131, reducing added cognitive complexity by 26.6%, and increasing Pass@1 by 2.3 points. However, these gains do not simply follow from a larger reasoning budget or larger models. We next ask whether minimal editing can be learned directly during post-training. We observe that supervised fine-tuning overfits to seen corruption patterns, whereas reinforcement learning gives the best out-of-domain edit-fidelity and performance-retention trade-off. These results position edit fidelity as a distinct axis of code-repair quality and show that it can be measured and learned.

title: Selective Hypergraph Refinement for Frozen Graph Clustering
abstract: Existing graph-clustering methods typically improve clustering performance by optimizing model parameters and node representations. Effective means of further improving the clustering results of an already trained and frozen model, however, remain limited. We study post-processing for frozen graph clustering. After checkpoint fixation, the procedure uses no labels and updates neither model parameters, node representations, nor the original graph structure. Instead, it exploits an attribute hypergraph to supplement higher-order relations that ordinary graphs cannot readily express, thereby refining existing cluster assignments. Because global hypergraph refinement can yield both performance gains and erroneous updates, we propose Selective Hypergraph Refinement (SHR). The method generates candidate residual directions from the hypergraph and evaluates their reliability using graph structure, node attributes, and matched-null evidence. It updates only nodes with sufficient support and otherwise retains their original assignments. Further analysis shows that whether a node changes cluster is jointly governed by its native assignment gap and the directional strength of the refinement. In a controlled common-suite evaluation, 13 of 15 backbone-dataset cells had a positive mean macro gain, one produced exact no-action, and one was negative. The cell-equal macro gain was 0.066 pp (95% bootstrap CI, [0.030, 0.107] pp), while only 0.209% of hard assignments changed on average. A broader 15-combination native-interface evaluation yielded a macro gain of 0.137 pp at a mean change ratio of 0.375%. These results indicate that frozen clustering outputs retain a limited but measurable refinement space after training. The effect is heterogeneous across backbone-dataset pairs, and broader coverage also increases exposure to negative transfer.

title: Teaching Surgeons the Semantic Web: A Five-Part Series from Wikidata to JSON-LD
abstract: This record archives a five-part teaching series that I published on LinkedIn between May 27 and September 1, 2026. The series teaches orthopedic surgeons how the semantic web works and how to connect their professional identity to it, moving from the knee replacement knowledge graph on Wikidata to the JSON-LD file on a practice website. The enclosed PDF reproduces the text of all five parts verbatim as posted, with the graphics attached to each post and with endnotes carrying the links from my author comments, including the Wikidata entities for the alignment, approach, and guidance techniques. Each part lists its publication date and canonical LinkedIn URL. The series is a companion to the Wikidata Knee Replacement Ecosphere dataset (concept DOI: 10.5281/zenodo.21852663) and its data descriptor preprint (DOI: 10.20944/preprints202608.1650.v1).

title: Title: Adaptive Chaos Dynamics for Optimal Algorithm Design
abstract: The pursuit of optimal algorithm design often necessitates meticulous parameter tuning, a process that frequently proves suboptimal due to inherent limitations in the input data. This research proposes a novel approach utilizing Adaptive Chaos Dynamics (ACD) to automatically refine algorithm parameters, fostering maximum efficiency and robustness across a diverse range of input data. Traditional optimization methods typically rely on fixed parameter sets, failing to capture the dynamic complexities of real-world scenarios. ACD, inspired by chaotic systems, dynamically adjusts parameters in real-time, mimicking the inherent unpredictability and self-organization of these systems. This system ensures an algorithm is always optimally tuned, surpassing the limitations of static parameter sets by embracing true adaptive learning. The core mechanism involves a feedback loop that continuously monitors input data and adjusts parameters to minimize error and maximize performance. This paper details the development of an ACD framework, explores its application to [mention a specific algorithm/problem domain, e.g., machine learning], and presents initial results demonstrating its efficacy in achieving superior performance metrics.

abstract: This paper introduces a novel quantum computing algorithm learning framework designed to dynamically adjust algorithm parameters based on training data characteristics. The framework is grounded in the principle of self-adaptation, allowing the algorithm to continuously refine its parameters to achieve optimal results. This work demonstrates the potential of quantum computing to significantly improve the performance of adaptive algorithms through dynamic parameter optimization.

title: Quantum Computing Foundation of High-Order Matrix Operations
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of utilizing quantum entanglement to revolutionize matrix operations, a crucial component of many linear algebra algorithms. The core claim is the development of a novel quantum computing approach that leverages quantum entanglement to accelerate complex linear algebra calculations. We propose a new algorithmic framework centered around quantum state manipulation, specifically designed to exploit the correlated properties of entangled qubits to significantly reduce computational complexity. This work will present a theoretical foundation for this approach, outlining the key mechanisms involved, and exploring the potential for practical implementation. The focus will be on demonstrating the theoretical benefits and providing a roadmap for future research.

title: Open Quantum Banking: Resource Theory and Dissipative Phase Transitions
abstract: We present an open quantum system formulation of the banking sector in which the dynamics are driven by a sequence of quantum instruments interspersed with continuous unitary evolution. The banking system interacts with a structured environment representing global markets, real‑economy sectors, and natural resources, modelled as finite‑dimensional qudits. Every primitive economic operation is a quantum instrument. For quadratic Hamiltonians, the moment hierarchy closes at second order, leading to a coupled system of equations for the mean values and the covariance matrix of Pauli operators. Near a symmetric equilibrium, the covariance dynamics reduce to a Lyapunov equation whose normal modes describe localised domestic and delocalised global financial cycles. We construct a resource theory of systemic entanglement (SER) based on the negativity, interpreted as a macro‑prudential indicator of exploitable quantum correlations. The central bank’s ancilla injection is identified as the unique non‑LOCC operation that can replenish this resource. We elucidate the economic meaning of LOCC, of high‑quality Bell pairs as perfect financial channels, and of bound entanglement, showing that a zero SER faithfully signals the absence of usable quantum advantage. By decomposing environmental qudits into qubits, pairwise PPT tests become sufficient, guaranteeing that the SER captures all distillable entanglement. We prove that the damping matrix enforces asymptotic stability of the covariance dynamics, so that only two genuine macroscopic phases exist: a correlated trading phase with positive SER, and a Zeno‑localised phase with vanishing SER; a crisis can only occur on the critical surface separating them. The shape of the critical line in the phase diagram is shown to depend on the ancilla–environment correlation matrix, which encodes the central bank’s injection policy. A simple taxonomy of policies and corresponding critical line topologies is derived. The central bank acts as an environment engineer by injecting ancillae and extracting entropy via weak measurements. The framework offers a rigorous, resource‑theoretic foundation for macro‑prudential policy, capital adequacy, and central bank digital currencies.

title: Self-Organizing Chaos of Quantum Entanglement-Driven
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum entanglement to drive self-organizing chaos, offering a novel approach to quantum computation. We propose a system based on entangled states, designed to guide the evolution of chaotic systems towards complex patterns through a carefully orchestrated quantum algorithm. The core claim is that leveraging entanglement's non-linear properties can significantly enhance the emergence of complex behavior within chaotic systems, ultimately leading to new computational capabilities. This work investigates the fundamental principles of this approach and presents a preliminary framework for utilizing entanglement to achieve this goal. The investigation focuses on the manipulation of entangled states to initiate and accelerate the formation of chaotic dynamics.

title: Rethinking Semantic Neural Network Learning Methods for Large AI Models: A Five‑Dimensional Potential‑Gradient Framework
abstract: This paper proposes a novel framework for evaluating and improving semantic transmission in large language models (LLMs) by introducing the concept of "semantic potential energy" derived from potential‑gradient and inversion analogies in physics. The author argues that semantic loss in human‑AI and human‑human communication is fundamentally a problem of asymmetric potential between sender and receiver, rather than a mere statistical fitting failure. The core contribution is a mathematical formulation: the total expressive potential $P_{\text{total}}$ is defined as the product of five normalized semantic dimensions—surface semantics, hidden/pragmatic semantics, logical coherence, factual grounding, and emotional fidelity—offset by dimension‑specific baselines, divided by a time‑penalty power law. This "five‑dimensional potential" model is inspired by the author's own teaching practice, where information loss is minimized by actively performing receiver‑side inversion at the sender side and compressing output into minimal mnemonic units. The paper presents sandbox simulation results using manually assigned dimension values, demonstrating that the model produces three decision tiers (PASS / REVIEW / BLOCK) corresponding to high, ambiguous, and low semantic potential states. The REVIEW tier is identified as the "inversion zone" where latent meaning must be decoded. All components are grounded in existing NLP evaluation tools (BERTScore, FactScore, NLI‑based pragmatic inference, etc.), but the specific combination—multiplicative aggregation of five dimensions with time decay and self‑consistency constraints—is, to the author's knowledge, previously unexplored. The paper explicitly acknowledges limitations: no real‑world LLM experiments were conducted due to resource constraints; threshold calibration is left as a reasonable interval rather than a physical constant; and hidden‑semantic continuous scoring remains an open engineering challenge. The framework is positioned not as a replacement for current alignment methods (RLHF, RAG), but as a complementary sender‑side evaluation protocol that could reduce semantic loss at the source. Code for the sandbox engine is provided. The author invites researchers with access to large‑scale dialogue datasets and computational resources to validate, extend, or refute the model. Keywords: semantic potential energy, large language models, potential gradient, inversion symmetry, sender‑side evaluation, semantic loss, sandbox simulation, five‑dimensional framework

title: Quantum Neural Network Dynamic Adjustment
abstract: This paper explores the potential of integrating quantum neural networks (QNNs) with dynamic adjustment mechanisms to enhance computational efficiency and accuracy. Traditional neural network parameter adjustments are often manual and limited in their adaptability, potentially hindering optimization. We propose a novel approach utilizing quantum entanglement and quantum simulation to automatically adjust network parameters during computation, offering a paradigm shift in neural network design. This investigation delves into the theoretical underpinnings of this dynamic adjustment, detailing the quantum algorithms employed and the expected benefits in terms of speed and precision. The paper concludes with a discussion of the challenges and future directions for this research.

title: ##基于多模态主动学习的动态知识图谱构建
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to dynamic knowledge graph construction leveraging multi-modal active learning. The core idea is to employ a reinforcement learning agent that actively explores and learns from visual, textual, and behavioral data to dynamically construct and update a knowledge graph. Unlike traditional knowledge graph construction methods that rely heavily on manual annotation or structured data extraction, our system proactively identifies knowledge gaps and prioritizes information acquisition based on the context of user queries. The system's architecture incorporates a reinforcement learning agent that selects which knowledge graph nodes and relationships to extract and add, guided by feedback from multiple modalities. The resulting knowledge graph exhibits dynamic adaptation, reflecting the influx of new information and evolving user needs. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a theoretical framework and outline the key components and algorithms involved. This research contributes to a more intelligent and adaptable knowledge graph system, paving the way for improved information retrieval and reasoning capabilities.

title: Adaptive Gradient Descent for Non-convex Optimization
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive gradient descent algorithm designed to efficiently optimize non-convex optimization problems. Traditional gradient descent methods often struggle with the presence of multiple local optima, hindering the search for global optima. Our approach dynamically adjusts the learning rate to mitigate this issue, thereby enhancing optimization efficiency and potentially leading to better solutions. We propose a mechanism that intelligently balances exploration and exploitation, systematically shifting the learning rate to navigate complex loss landscapes. The core of the algorithm involves a novel update rule predicated on a dynamic learning rate adjustment strategy. The paper details the theoretical foundations, implementation, and experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of this adaptive method in a range of non-convex optimization tasks. We highlight the benefits of this approach compared to standard gradient descent, particularly in scenarios where local optima are prevalent.

title: Causal Discovery via Bayesian Networks with Hidden Markov Models
abstract: This paper introduces a novel approach to causal discovery leveraging the strengths of Bayesian Networks and Hidden Markov Models (HMMs). Existing causal discovery algorithms often falter when dealing with complex, time-varying dependencies inherent in many real-world systems. Our method addresses this limitation by integrating Bayesian Network inference with HMMs to explicitly model temporal dynamics and subsequently infer causal relationships from sequential data. The core claim is that by incorporating temporal structure, we achieve a more robust and accurate understanding of causal dependencies. We present a framework for constructing Bayesian Networks augmented with HMMs, detailing the inference process and outlining the key steps involved in discovering causal relationships from time-series data. The proposed method offers a significant advancement in causal discovery, particularly for systems exhibiting temporal evolution and intricate dependencies. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through a theoretical analysis and a conceptual outline, paving the way for future empirical validation.

title: Adaptive Machine Learning Model Parameter Adjustment Strategy
abstract: This paper introduces a novel adaptive machine learning model parameter adjustment strategy leveraging machine learning models to automatically optimize model parameters based on data characteristics. Traditional parameter tuning methods often require manual intervention, which can be time-consuming and potentially suboptimal. Our proposed approach utilizes a trained machine learning model to learn and adapt to the data distribution, resulting in improved predictive accuracy and stability compared to traditional methods. This work addresses the limitations of existing parameter tuning techniques by introducing a self-learning mechanism that dynamically adjusts model parameters based on the inherent data structure. We detail the algorithm's architecture, training process, and performance evaluation, demonstrating its effectiveness in various scenarios. The core claim highlights the key advantage of this adaptive strategy – a more precise and automated approach to parameter tuning.

This paper introduces a quantum-driven constraint propagation algorithm designed to explore the vast search space of possible algorithm designs, identifying previously unseen patterns and dramatically improving algorithm performance. We explore the potential of quantum superposition and entanglement to enhance the search process, leading to faster convergence and the discovery of innovative algorithmic solutions. The core mechanism focuses on dynamically adjusting the constraint propagation strategy based on quantum-enhanced measurements, ensuring a focused exploration of the relevant search space. The results demonstrate significant improvements in algorithm efficiency compared to classical constraint propagation methods, particularly in complex search spaces.

title: Quantum Error Correction via Adaptive Resonance Networks
abstract: Quantum error correction is a critical challenge in quantum computing, demanding highly sophisticated techniques to protect quantum information from decoherence and errors. This paper explores the application of Adaptive Resonance Networks (ARNs) as a novel quantum error correction scheme. We propose a system where the ARN dynamically adjusts its network parameters to optimize for minimizing error rates, tailored to specific qubit configurations. This approach leverages the inherent adaptability of neural networks to enhance error correction efficiency and robustness. The core mechanism involves a neural network-inspired architecture that learns and adapts to the observed error patterns, offering a potentially more efficient and robust strategy compared to traditional approaches. The paper details the design of the ARN, its operational methodology, and preliminary results demonstrating its effectiveness in mitigating errors.

title: Visualizing the Training Process of MLP
abstract: Multilayer Perceptrons (MLPs) are extensively used in many machine learning applications; yet, because of their high dimensionality and complexity, their training process is still largely opaque. In order to better understand how MLPs learn and modify their internal representations, this study focuses on visualizing the evolution of decision boundaries during training. We gain insights into neural networks' learning dynamics and convergence behavior by analyzing how the decision regions change as training progresses. This work also contributes to the broader field of Explainable AI (XAI) by offering a visual approach to interpreting neural network decision-making, addressing the common critique of MLPs being black-box models.

title: A first exercise in quantum computing for molecular chemistry: the hydrogen molecule cation
abstract: Abstract Chemical simulation is expected to be one of the first practical applications of real quantum computers. Therefore, curricular materials should be developed to teach students the fundamentals of this very important topic. Even the simplest molecule, diatomic hydrogen, is tremendously complicated to simulate with a quantum computer. Much of the complexity is due to the interaction of the two electrons. As a first warm-up exercise in quantum computing for chemistry, we show how to simulate the hydrogen molecule cation, which has only one electron.

title: A context-aware dynamic model selection framework based on proximal policy optimization for day-ahead PV power forecasting
abstract: To enhance the accuracy of day-ahead photovoltaic (PV) power forecasting and overcome the limited adaptability of individual models under varying weather conditions, this paper proposes a scenario-aware dynamic model selection method based on an actor-critic contextual policy learning approach. The approach first performs cluster analysis on temporal features extracted from meteorological variables that influence PV output, classifying historical weather patterns into four typical scenarios: clear, partly cloudy, overcast, and rainy. A forecasting model library comprising multiple deep learning architectures is then constructed. A reinforcement learning agent based on Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) is trained to learn an optimal policy that dynamically selects the most suitable model from the library according to the day-ahead meteorological features of the target day. By adaptively matching the optimal model to the specific characteristics of each target day, the proposed method substantially improves prediction accuracy. Experimental results on real-world PV data show that the proposed method effectively leverages the complementary strengths of multiple models. Compared with the static optimal strategy, it reduces RMSE by 13.97% overall. These results demonstrate its strong effectiveness and adaptability to complex and variable weather scenarios.

title: The Native-Signature Boundary in Post-Quantum Distributed Authorization
abstract: Post-quantum signature migration poses a distinct systems problem when authorization is distributed among multiple parties. In native threshold signing, the signature algorithm may determine key generation, share state, preprocessing, interaction, combination, refresh, and recovery. Architectures that evaluate threshold policy outside the native signing relation can reduce this coupling, but their authorization evidence is not accepted by an unchanged native verifier unless a trusted complete-key signer translates approval into a native signature. This paper organizes that design boundary through three properties: native-signature compatibility, unilateral-signing resistance, and threshold-layer agility. We classify specialized threshold signatures, generic MPC signing, distributed hash-based constructions, programmable multisignature and dual-gate authorization, and threshold-authorized HSM signing. A migration impact surface identifies which components change with the signature algorithm. Across the surveyed families, no design simultaneously provides native output, unilateral-signing resistance, and threshold-layer agility. This is an architectural tension, not an impossibility claim, and it clarifies why a replaceable API alone does not make distributed authorization cryptographically agile.

title: Floquetifying stabiliser codes with distance-preserving rewrites
abstract: Stabiliser codes with large weight measurements can be challenging to implement fault-tolerantly. To overcome this, we propose a Floquetification procedure which, given a stabiliser code, synthesises a novel Floquet code that only uses single- and two-qubit operations. Moreover, this procedure preserves the distance and number of logicals of the original code. The new Floquet code requires additional physical qubits. This overhead is linear in the weight of the largest measurement of the original code. Our method is based on the ZX calculus, a graphical language for representing and rewriting quantum circuits. However, a problem arises with the use of ZX in the context of rewriting error-correcting codes: ZX rewrites generally do not preserve code distance. Tackling this issue, we define the notion of distance-preserving rewrite that enables the transformation of error-correcting codes without changing their distance. These distance-preserving rewrites are used to decompose arbitrary weight stabiliser measurements into quantum circuits with single- and two-qubit operations. As we only use distance-preserving rewrites, we are guaranteed that a single error in the resulting circuit creates at most a single error on the data qubits. These decompositions enable us to generalise the Floquetification procedure of Townsend-Teague et al \cite{townsend-teagueFloquetifyingColourCode2023} to arbitrary stabiliser codes, provably preserving the distance and number of logicals of the original code.

title: REFINE: LLM Refinement over Budgeted Text-Attributed Graphs for Personalized Medical Concept Representation
abstract: Learning rich medical concept representations is essential for EHR prediction. Text-attributed knowledge graphs (TKGs) provide a natural foundation by organizing heterogeneous medical relations together with textual semantics. However, most existing encoders process concepts uniformly across patients, despite the fact that a code's meaning and predictive value depend on patient-specific clinical context and trajectory. Learning patient-personalized concept representations from TKGs introduces two key challenges: (1) deciding how much KG context to incorporate for each observed code, and (2) aligning semantic information with the patient-specific relational structure. We propose REFINE, a KG-aware budgeted LLM graph refinement framework for patient-personalized medical concept encoding. Starting from a global TKG, REFINE constructs patient-specific temporal graphs. A sequential reinforcement learning policy selects a personalized KG expansion budget for each observed code. The resulting patient graph is processed by a heterogeneous GNN to capture relation-aware structural dependencies, while a frozen LLM uses graph-aware soft prompts to semantically refine concept representations. Experiments on MIMIC-III and MIMIC-IV show that REFINE consistently improves diverse EHR backbones, outperforms strong baselines, and demonstrates robust gains across component ablation, KG selection, and data insufficiency.

title: LLaDA-Image: Building Strong Image Generators with Fully Open Training Recipes
abstract: We introduce LLaDA-Image, a unified framework that pairs a 6B Diffusion Transformer (DiT) trained from scratch with a frozen vision-language understanding module built on the LLaDA2.0-Mini diffusion language model backbone. Instead of relying heavily on paired image-text data from the beginning, we first build a strong visual generative prior through image-only pre-training and mid-training. The generation pipeline comprises 220M samples, 98 of which are real images. For efficient and scalable optimization, we use parameter-free RMSNorm throughout the DiT together with the Muon optimizer. The resulting unified model produces highly photorealistic images while accurately following fine-grained editing instructions. We further distill LLaDA-Image into LLaDA-Image-Turbo, enabling fast inference in 2-4 sampling steps. On Qwen-Image-Bench, LLaDA-Image achieves overall scores of 53.53 and 53.38 on the English and Chinese tracks, respectively, setting a new state-of-the-art among open-source models on both tracks. To support further research on capable and efficient generative models, we release our model weights, training code, and detailed recipes.

title: Deep Learning for Financial Fraud Detection: A Hybrid GNN-Transformer Fraud Detection Model
abstract: Financial fraud has become a major challenge in modern digital banking and online financial systems. Traditional fraud detection systems are unable to detect complex and rapidly changing fraudulent activities efficiently. Deep learning techniques provide intelligent solutions by automatically learning hidden transaction patterns and detecting anomalies in real time. This study presents a comprehensive review of deep learning methods used in financial fraud detection, including Convolution Neural Networks (CNN)[1], Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM), Autoencoders, Graph Neural Networks (GNN), and Transformer models. A new hybrid fraud detection framework combining Graph Neural Networks and Transformer architecture is proposed to improve fraud detection accuracy and reduce false positives. The proposed model effectively handles imbalanced financial datasets using SMOTE and anomaly-based learning techniques. Experimental analysis shows improved performance in terms of accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and AUC. The research concludes that hybrid deep learning models can significantly improve financial fraud detection systems in banking, insurance, and online transaction environments.

title: Correlated Qubit Degradation Events and Their Physical Classification from Cloud Quantum Processor Telemetry
authors: Life Sim Technologies, Inc., Amelia, Ohio, USA
abstract: We analyze 10.4 million calibration measurements from three IBM Heron superconducting quantumprocessors and identify two physically distinct classes of correlated multi-qubit degradationevents using only routine cloud-accessible telemetry. A column-wise permutation test reveals statisticallysignificant excess of simultaneous T1 crashes (42.8× expected at ≥ 10 simultaneous,p < 0.0001), simultaneous T2 crashes (4.8× at ≥ 10, p < 0.001), and simultaneous CZ gate-errorspikes (23.4× at ≥ 20, p < 0.0001; excess reaching 15,000× at ≥ 30). All three signals replicateacross backends (Fisher combined p < 10−7). Classifying high-crash snapshots by which parametersdegrade reveals two event types: Type A events degrade T1, T2, and CZ gate fidelity simultaneously(Cohen’s d = −0.94 for crashed-qubit T2), consistent with quasiparticle poisoning from high-energyparticle impacts; Type B events degrade T2 alone without affecting T1 or gate errors, consistentwith correlated dephasing noise. Type B events recover more slowly than Type A, persisting overmultiple calibration cycles with the same qubits remaining affected. T1-only events are rare acrossbackends, consistent with the expectation that relaxation degradation typically accompanies dephasing.Different qubits crash each time (mean Jaccard similarity ≤ 0.04), and readout fidelityremains unaffected in both event types. These correlated events—previously detectable only withdedicated particle detectors—are identifiable, classifiable, and operationally actionable from existingcloud calibration data without hardware modification.

title: Dynamic Topographic Neural Networks
abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Topographic Neural Networks (DTNN), a novel neural network architecture that departs from traditional, static topological structures. The core innovation lies in the network's ability to dynamically adjust the connection strengths between neurons based on incoming data. DTNN utilizes a reinforcement learning framework where each neuron possesses a "topographic radius," which governs the range of connections it establishes. This radius is not pre-determined but rather adapts in real-time based on both the input signal intensity and error feedback. This dynamic adjustment allows the network to self-organize and optimize its topology for specific tasks. The paper details the mathematical formulation of the DTNN, including the reinforcement learning objective, the topographic radius update rule, and the connection strength adjustment mechanism. evidence.title: Dynamic Topographic Neural Networks
evidence.abstract: This paper introduces Dynamic Topographic Neural Networks (DTNN), a novel neural network architecture that departs from traditional, static topological structures. The core innovation lies in the network's ability to dynamically adjust the connection strengths between neurons based on incoming data. title: Predictive Coding of Temporal Symbolic Sequences
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to modeling temporal symbolic sequences by leveraging the principles of predictive coding and incorporating differentiable symbolic reasoning. Traditional recurrent neural networks (RNNs) often falter in capturing the intricate hierarchical structures inherent in symbolic sequences, primarily due to their reliance on continuous representations and difficulty in explicitly encoding abstract symbolic relationships. Our framework addresses this limitation through a hierarchical predictive coding architecture where higher-level units predict the symbols generated by lower-level units. The prediction errors generated during this process are then utilized to refine the model's representation and learn a hierarchical structure. Crucially, we integrate a differentiable symbolic interpreter to facilitate symbolic reasoning within the network, allowing it to explicitly manipulate and understand symbolic relationships. This combination enables the model to not only predict the next symbol in a sequence but also to reason about the underlying symbolic structure, leading to a more robust and efficient representation of temporal symbolic sequences. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through theoretical analysis and outline the key components, including the predictive coding architecture, the differentiable symbolic interpreter, and the error-driven learning mechanism. The core contribution lies in seamlessly integrating predictive coding with symbolic reasoning, creating a system capable of capturing and exploiting the hierarchical nature of symbolic sequences for improved temporal prediction and understanding.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Program Synthesis via Bayesian Optimization of Neural Circuit Design
abstract: Neural program synthesis aims to automatically generate programs from examples, offering a promising approach to bridging the gap between symbolic reasoning and neural network learning. However, existing methods often suffer from brittleness and a lack of systematic exploration of the vast design space. This research introduces a novel neuro-symbolic framework for program synthesis, leveraging Bayesian optimization to iteratively refine neural circuit designs. The core idea is to combine the pattern recognition capabilities of neural networks with the logical reasoning of symbolic systems within a closed-loop optimization process. Bayesian optimization guides the design of neural circuits, incorporating symbolic constraints and logical rules to ensure the generated programs satisfy desired specifications. The system learns both the neural network architecture and the underlying program logic simultaneously. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach through a series of simulations, showcasing its ability to synthesize programs with greater robustness and efficiency compared to traditional methods. Key metrics include the success rate of program synthesis, the complexity of the generated circuits, and the adherence to specified logical constraints. The system achieves significant improvements in these areas through the intelligent combination of these two paradigms.

title: Quantum Simulation for Materials Science Computation
abstract: This paper explores the potential of quantum simulation for materials science computation. Traditional computational methods often struggle with the inherent quantum nature of materials, leading to inaccuracies in predicting their properties. Quantum simulation offers a promising alternative by directly simulating quantum systems using quantum computers. This work details the core concept, mechanism, and potential impact of leveraging quantum computers to accurately model and predict material behavior. The core claim is that utilizing quantum computers for materials quantum simulation will lead to more precise material property predictions and accelerate materials research. The fundamental mechanism involves constructing a quantum simulator, employing qubits to represent and simulate the quantum system of a material, enabling the calculation of material properties. This research highlights the novel application of quantum simulation in materials science, providing a pathway towards improved material prediction capabilities.

title: Algorithmic Information Theory for Neural Network Robustness
abstract: This paper investigates the vulnerability of neural networks to adversarial attacks through the lens of algorithmic information theory. The core concept is that the inherent information content within a neural network's learned representations dictates its robustness. We propose a metric based on Kolmogorov complexity – a measure of the shortest program required to generate a given string – to quantify the compressibility of hidden state representations. A lower Kolmogorov complexity implies a more robust representation, resistant to small perturbations that can trigger adversarial misclassifications. The research outlines a training paradigm focused on minimizing this compressibility metric, thereby enhancing the network's resilience. This approach represents a novel application of algorithmic information theory, offering a fundamentally different perspective on neural network robustness compared to traditional methods.

title: Title: Quantum Entanglement Resonance Mapping (QERM)
abstract: Quantum entanglement, a cornerstone of quantum mechanics, exhibits correlations that defy classical intuition. However, the precise nature of these correlations – particularly the subtle ones – remains largely enigmatic. This research proposes a novel quantum entanglement resonance mapping (QERM) technique, aiming to transcend current limitations in detection and analysis by dynamically adapting a multi-frequency resonant field to create a unique 'signature' for entanglement. This signature will exceed existing detection capabilities, offering insights into fundamental constraints on quantum information transfer and potentially revolutionizing our understanding of entanglement. The core mechanism relies on exploiting the vibrational properties of entangled particles to generate a detectable pattern, offering a fundamentally different approach than conventional statistical analysis. This paper details the theoretical framework, algorithm design, and preliminary experimental validation of QERM, highlighting its potential for groundbreaking advancements in quantum research.

title: Meta-Learning for Automated Algorithm Selection and Hyperparameter Tuning
abstract: This paper explores the application of meta-learning techniques to the automated selection of machine learning algorithms and their corresponding hyperparameters. The core idea is to leverage past experience – specifically, the performance of different algorithms on various tasks – to train a meta-learner. This meta-learner then learns a policy that maps task descriptions (e.g., data characteristics, problem type) to optimal algorithm and hyperparameter configurations. We demonstrate the potential for significantly improving efficiency and performance in machine learning workflows by automating a traditionally manual and often time-consuming process. The research focuses on the theoretical underpinnings and conceptual framework, providing a foundation for future development and experimentation. The key contributions lie in establishing a systematic approach to meta-learning for algorithm selection and hyperparameter tuning, offering a novel way to adapt algorithms to specific problems.

title: Cognitive Graph Databases for Human-AI Interaction
abstract: This paper proposes a novel approach to human-AI interaction by leveraging cognitive graph databases. Traditional graph databases struggle to replicate the cognitive processes of humans, leading to cumbersome and unintuitive interactions. This research introduces a graph database architecture explicitly designed to incorporate cognitive models – memory hierarchies (M), attention mechanisms (A), and knowledge representation (K) – to bridge the gap between human and AI understanding. The core claim is that traditional graph databases lack the necessary cognitive capabilities for seamless interaction. The proposed mechanism involves designing a graph database optimized for collaborative work between humans and AI, utilizing these cognitive models to create a more intuitive and efficient system. We define the interaction as follows: Let *I* represent the interaction, *H* represent the human, and *AI* represent the artificial intelligence. The goal is to maximize the efficiency of *I* between *H* and *AI*. We can represent the interaction as: *I* = *f*( *H*, *AI*, M, A, K). The effectiveness of this function is measured by the reduction in the number of steps required to complete a task, and the improvement in the accuracy of the task. The proposed system aims to reduce the complexity of this function by integrating cognitive models. This paper outlines the design principles and key components of this cognitive graph database and discusses its potential impact on various human-AI applications.

abstract: This paper presents a novel quantum algorithm optimization approach utilizing a dynamically adjusted quantum graph. Traditional optimization methods often rely on manual parameter tuning, limiting the algorithm's adaptability. This work proposes a quantum graph-based framework where the graph itself evolves during the optimization process, allowing for continuous refinement and improved performance. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this method through a series of benchmark quantum algorithms, showcasing its ability to achieve state-of-the-art results with reduced computational cost. The core mechanism leverages the inherent properties of quantum graphs to dynamically adjust path lengths and interactions, ultimately leading to enhanced algorithm efficiency.

title: On Self-Organization of Quantum Networks Based on Multi-Agent Learning
abstract: This paper investigates the application of multi-agent learning (MAL) for the self-organization and optimization of quantum networks. Traditional approaches to quantum network design and management often rely on manual configuration or predefined protocols, which can be inefficient and inflexible. We propose a framework where individual nodes within the quantum network are treated as intelligent agents, leveraging the principles of MAL to dynamically adapt the network's topology and resource allocation. The core of the approach lies in utilizing MAL algorithms to enable the quantum network to autonomously learn optimal configurations based on network conditions and performance metrics. This paper details the theoretical foundation, proposes a specific MAL architecture, and outlines the key components necessary for implementation. The potential benefits of this approach include enhanced network resilience, improved resource utilization, and ultimately, increased overall quantum network performance. The presented model provides a novel pathway towards scalable and adaptable quantum network architectures. ---

title: Program Synthesis via Simulated Annealing
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to program synthesis utilizing the Simulated Annealing (SA) algorithm. The core idea is to formulate the program synthesis problem as a search space within the SA framework, allowing for automated generation of programs that fulfill specified functional requirements. Traditional program synthesis techniques often struggle with complexity and efficiency, particularly when dealing with intricate specifications. This work demonstrates that SA's probabilistic search strategy can effectively navigate this complex landscape, leading to the discovery of optimal or near-optimal program solutions. The presented method offers a promising alternative for automating program generation, reducing development time and potentially uncovering more efficient code than manually crafted solutions. We detail the core algorithm, its implementation, and illustrate its potential with a simplified example. ---

title: Based on Multi-Modal Data Fusion for Causal Inference Framework
abstract: This paper introduces a novel framework for causal inference leveraging the fusion of multi-modal data. The core claim is that integrating information from diverse sources, such as images, text, and audio, significantly enhances the accuracy of causal inference and reveals previously hidden causal relationships. The proposed mechanism utilizes a Bayesian network-based multi-modal data fusion framework coupled with causal inference algorithms for model learning. This approach addresses the limitations of traditional causal inference methods that often rely on single-source data, providing a more robust and nuanced understanding of complex systems. The framework aims to improve the reliability of causal discovery by considering the interdependencies between different data modalities. This research contributes a new methodology for causal inference, offering potential advancements in fields requiring robust understanding of complex systems where multiple types of data exist.

title: Neuro-Symbolic Reasoning for Commonsense Knowledge
abstract: This paper presents a novel approach to commonsense reasoning by integrating neural networks and symbolic reasoning engines within a unified neuro-symbolic framework. The core challenge lies in the limitations of neural networks in effectively utilizing and applying commonsense knowledge. Current deep learning models often excel at pattern recognition but lack the ability to perform logical inference and reason with implicit assumptions that are fundamental to human understanding. This work addresses this gap by proposing a system that leverages the strengths of both paradigms. The neural component focuses on extracting relevant features and patterns from data, while the symbolic component provides a mechanism for logical deduction and knowledge representation. Specifically, we introduce a hybrid architecture where a neural network processes raw sensory input to generate a set of potential hypotheses, which are then evaluated and refined by a symbolic reasoning engine utilizing a knowledge graph. The system's ability to seamlessly transition between perceptual understanding and logical inference is crucial for robust and explainable reasoning in complex, real-world scenarios. The results demonstrate a significant improvement in the accuracy and interpretability of commonsense reasoning compared to solely neural or purely symbolic approaches. Ultimately, this research contributes to the development of more intelligent and trustworthy AI systems.

title: Quantum-Inspired Evolutionary Algorithms for Optimization
abstract: This paper investigates the potential of incorporating quantum mechanical concepts into evolutionary algorithms (EAs) to improve their optimization capabilities. Traditional EAs, while effective, often struggle with complex search spaces and can get trapped in local optima. We propose a framework for developing quantum-inspired EAs that leverages principles such as superposition and entanglement to enhance exploration and exploitation strategies. The core idea is to introduce probabilistic operators and adaptive parameter control mimicking quantum behaviors. We present a detailed description of the proposed algorithm, focusing on the mathematical formulation of the key components, including the representation of solutions, the selection process, and the mutation operator. The algorithm's performance is evaluated on several benchmark optimization problems, demonstrating its potential to outperform conventional EAs in scenarios demanding high accuracy and rapid convergence. Furthermore, we analyze the theoretical implications of this approach, highlighting the advantages derived from quantum-inspired mechanisms. This work contributes to the ongoing research at the intersection of evolutionary computation and quantum information theory, offering a novel approach to tackling complex optimization challenges.

title: Title: Non-Local Graph Embedding for Semantic Similarity
abstract: This paper investigates the application of non-local graph embedding techniques to enhance semantic similarity calculations. Traditional graph embedding methods often struggle with capturing the intricate relationships between distant nodes, limiting the accuracy of similarity assessments. We propose a novel approach that leverages quantum-inspired principles to construct a graph representation capable of more effectively modeling these complex connections. The core mechanism centers around dynamically weighting edges based on a learned latent representation, allowing the model to better represent the semantic context of nodes even across significant distances. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this technique through a series of experiments, showcasing significant improvements in similarity metrics across diverse datasets, particularly in scenarios involving nuanced relationships. The results highlight the potential of this approach to overcome limitations of existing methods and achieve more robust semantic similarity assessments.

The paper details the core components of the ATL framework, including the topology transformation process, the adaptive parameter adjustment algorithm, and the resulting improvements in model performance and generalization. title: Dynamic Quantum拓扑结构下的拓扑信息预测 (Dynamic Topology-Based Quantum Computation Topology Prediction)
abstract: Quantum computation, a paradigm shift in computation, relies heavily on the manipulation of quantum states. However, the intricate nature of quantum systems necessitates sophisticated techniques for topology prediction, a crucial element in understanding quantum computation's behavior and potential. This paper explores the application of dynamic topology, a novel approach to structure optimization, to predict topology information of quantum computation, ultimately aiming to optimize quantum computation parameters. Traditional methods often involve manual parameter selection, limiting adaptability and hindering the exploration of diverse quantum configurations. We propose a model leveraging dynamic topology to automatically generate optimal quantum computation parameters, resulting in enhanced performance and a deeper understanding of quantum systems. This work presents a framework for predicting topology information using dynamic topology, offering a significant advancement in topology-based optimization for quantum computation.

title: A novel deep learning-based fraud detection framework integrating autonomous PSO-GA-based feature selection, hyperparameter optimization, and explainable artificial intelligence
abstract: Fraud detection is a critical component of financial security, aiming to accurately distinguish fraudulent transactions from the vast volume of legitimate financial activities. However, this task remains highly challenging because fraudsters continuously evolve their attack strategies to circumvent existing security mechanisms, while the severe class imbalance inherent in transaction datasets further degrades detection performance. Although numerous approaches have been proposed, a robust, accurate, and interpretable fraud detection system has not yet been successfully developed. This paper suggests a novel hybrid deep learning framework for fraud detection as a solution to these problems. The primary contribution of this work is the development of a hybrid framework featuring an autonomous optimization mechanism that dynamically selects between Particle Swarm Optimization (PSO) and Genetic Algorithm (GA) for hyperparameter optimization and feature selection, deep learning (DL) models for fraud classification, and an Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) layer integrating Grad-CAM, SHAP and LIME to provide both global and local interpretations of model decisions. The proposed methodology consists of four main stages: data preprocessing, metaheuristic-based hyperparameter optimization and feature subset selection, transaction classification using DL and machine learning (ML) models, and XAI-based interpretability analysis. The proposed framework was thoroughly tested on the 284,807 transactions of the European cardholder fraud dataset and the BankSim Credit Card Payment Dataset, and contrasted with a number of cutting-edge methods. Experimental results demonstrate that the XAI-enabled PSO-optimized LSTM framework trained on the compact 14-feature subset (α3) consistently outperformed all competing models and achieved the most favorable balance between computational efficiency, predictive performance, robustness, false positive reduction, and interpretability. The proposed model attained an AUC-ROC of 0.9954, an F1-score of 93.65%, a precision of 95.62% and an accuracy of 99.96%, outperforming cutting-edge methods while providing a computationally efficient and more reliable solution for fraud detection.

title: LLM-Aided Design for Manufacturing: A Multi-Agent System for Intent-Preserving Redesign of CAD for Improved Manufacturability
abstract: We introduce autonomous, intent-preserving Design for Manufacturing (DFM) redesign of CAD parts: given an engineer's CAD model, the method returns a variant that is easier to manufacture without losing its design intent. Generating such a redesign in a single shot is unreliable, since CAD fidelity degrades as parts grow complex; we instead produce it as a sequence of individually verified design transitions. Our DFM-Redesign pipeline realizes this with two coupled agent subsystems driven by a pretrained multimodal LLM: a DFM Reviewer that inspects the current design and proposes one intent-preserving manufacturability improvement at a time, and a CAD Modifier that executes each proposal as an edit to the part's CadQuery program. The CAD Modifier closes a verification loop, compiling every candidate edit and visually checking it against the intended change from multi-view renderings, then re-generating or re-instructing until the edit is accepted or abandoned. Iterating review and verified modification compounds edits into parts more complex than one-shot generators reliably produce, preserves the original intent at each step, and requires no fine-tuning. On a 46-part benchmark scored by chamfer distance to reference geometries, the CAD Modifier reproduces target parts more accurately on average than chain-of-thought single agents given the same tools, and ablations isolate the contributions of the visual review loop and of captioning the design state before each edit. A centrifugal pump casing built from 32 chained transitions illustrates the complexity reachable by compounding verified edits. This is a preliminary report: evaluation of the full review-and-redesign loop, including manufacturability gain and an operational measure of intent preservation, is ongoing.

title: Beyond Majority Vote: Multi-Perspective Adjudication for Medical Hallucination Detection
abstract: Understanding the frequency of factual errors in chatbot-generated text and evaluating systems that detect these errors is critical for determining chatbot safety. Yet factual-error detection is often treated as a single-pass, single-annotator labeling problem. In long-form chatbot responses, factual errors can be subtle and embedded within mostly correct text. We develop a multi-perspective annotation study of medically relevant chatbot responses, combining first-pass annotation, LLM-as-a-Judge (LaJ) candidate discovery, and two forms of adjudication: medical-expert and evidence-based fact-checking. First-pass annotators frequently miss factual errors later validated by adjudicators. LaJ improves candidate discovery, but is insufficient on its own: It misses factual errors that annotators catch. We also find disagreement among adjudicators, suggesting that adjudication over multiple candidate sources can improve benchmark completeness, but does not eliminate the need to apply judgment and expertise. Applied to an existing benchmark, this technique reveals a similar pattern of missing annotations. Together, these results suggest that in the settings examined here, single-pass hallucination benchmarks may achieve scale at the cost of undercounting factual errors. Multi-pass adjudication can improve coverage, but inferences drawn from the benchmarks are still sensitive to the judgment, expertise, and evidence used to determine error presence.

title: ARCOS: Zero-shot Boundary Localization for Corneal Layer Segmentation Across Optical Coherence Tomography Devices
abstract: Accurate segmentation of corneal layers in optical coherence tomography (OCT) is essential for quantitative assessment of corneal morphology, including layer thickness and structural changes associated with disease or surgery. However, automatic segmentation remains challenging because corneal interfaces are thin, affected by speckle noise, and variable across acquisition devices. In this work, we propose ARCOS, a patch-based zero-shot boundary localization framework for corneal layer segmentation in clinical anterior-segment OCT images. Rather than performing conventional region classification, the method predicts boundary heatmaps for the main corneal interfaces from overlapping native-resolution patches. Patch-level predictions are stitched across the full B-scan and converted into boundary locations to obtain continuous, anatomically ordered layer segmentations. The network combines multi-scale feature fusion with a self-conditioned refinement module that uses intermediate boundary information to improve local heatmap predictions while preserving spatial detail. The method was evaluated on clinical OCT images acquired from multiple devices and compared with representative segmentation baselines using boundary localization and derived thickness metrics. The proposed method achieved an off-by-one boundary localization accuracy of 95.1% and a mean absolute boundary error of 0.514 pixels on the matched-device test set. In zero-shot cross-device evaluation, it maintained an average off-by-one accuracy of 84.3% and a mean absolute boundary error of 0.855 pixels across unseen acquisition devices, outperforming the baseline models. Thickness estimates derived from the predicted boundaries showed low error across corneal regions, supporting the method's use for quantitative corneal OCT analysis.

title: Proportional infinite-width infinite-depth limit for deep linear neural networks
abstract: In this paper, we study the distributional properties of linear neural networks with random parameters in the context of large networks, where the number of layers diverges in proportion to the number of neurons per layer. Prior works have shown that in the infinite-width regime, where the number of neurons per layer grows to infinity while the depth remains fixed, neural networks converge to a Gaussian process, known as the Neural Network Gaussian Process. However, this Gaussian limit sacrifices descriptive power, as it lacks the ability to learn dependent features and produce output correlations that reflect observed labels. Motivated by these limitations, we explore the joint proportional limit in which both depth and width diverge but maintain a constant ratio, yielding a non-Gaussian distribution that retains correlations between outputs. Our contribution extends previous works by explicitly characterizing, for linear activation functions, the limiting distribution at the level of the entire network process as a nontrivial mixture of Gaussians processes.

title: Editable Visual Design
abstract: While diffusion base models such as GPT-Image-2 and Nano-Banana exhibit remarkable visual expressiveness, their end-to-end generation inherently yields flattened bitmaps with error-prone text, precluding layer-wise post-editing. Conversely, code-based visual generation via Coding Agents provides precise layout control and decoupled layers, yet remains constrained by a lack of global aesthetic intuition and the difficulty of coding complex visual assets. To address this, we propose Editable Visual Design, a new paradigm driven by a Coding Agent. We designate the VLM as the ``creative brain'' for requirement comprehension, task planning, and aesthetic judgment, while utilizing the image generation model as an on-demand ``visual world simulator'' to synthesize standalone visual assets. Operating under an ``imagine first, then act'' closed-loop workflow, the agent generates isolated assets, writes native HTML/CSS, and iteratively refines the design against visual rendering feedback. Furthermore, Agent Design Replay faithfully reproduces the creative and reasoning trajectory akin to that of professional human designers. Ultimately, the system delivers editable artifacts with decoupled layers and real text, enabling users to perform intuitive mouse dragging and layout adjustments on a graphical user interface. Validations on posters, infographics, and other scenarios show that this paradigm successfully achieves both refined aesthetics and production-grade editability.

title: The Dually Flat Geometry of Planning as Inference
abstract: We present an alternative characterization of the occupancy measure of reinforcement learning, obtained by embedding the planning criterion into the dynamics through a resetting planning process. Its stationary measure, which we term visitation measure, is the object on which the information geometry of decision making is most naturally expressed. The achievable visitation measures form a dually flat statistical manifold whose two affine charts are the visitation probabilities and the log-policies, dual under the conditional entropy. This structure makes planning-as-inference generalize from linear rewards to nonlinear functionals of the visitation, each iterate solved by one natural-gradient step, and gives the temporal-difference error the interpretation of a marginal-utility estimate. We develop the geometry and its consequences for reinforcement learning and theoretical neuroscience.

title: Conformity Breaks Conformal Prediction
abstract: A conformal certificate can be valid when an LLM answers alone and invalid when the same LLM sees peers that unanimously assert a wrong answer. The question is unchanged; the model's score for the correct answer changes. We call this a score-mechanism shift: clean calibration certifies how the model scores answers alone, but not how it scores them under peer pressure. We show that this shift silently breaks conformal prediction in multi-agent LLM systems. Across open-weight models and multiple-choice QA tasks, coverage falls from a calibrated 90% to 74% under unanimous-wrong peers at the standard alpha = 0.10 operating point. The average hides a sharper failure: by targeting the low-confidence items the certificate still covers, an attacker nearly halves coverage on that subgroup, from 87% to 47%, while the monitored average remains much higher. The failure also reaches the decision layer: a system that should escalate when uncertain can instead become confident enough to act on the attacker's wrong answer. Standard conformal fixes do not solve the problem, because the question distribution has not changed; the model's scoring behavior has.

title: Translation as a Decision Space: A Multi-Agent Perspective on Low-Resource Dialect Generation
abstract: Neural machine translation (NMT) systems typically produce a single output per input, obscuring the alternative decision trajectories implicitly available within multilingual decoding. This opacity becomes particularly problematic in low-resource dialect settings, where multiple linguistically valid realizations may differ in lexical authenticity, register, and structural stability. We propose reframing translation as a structured decision space explored by autonomous translation agents. Instead of analyzing a single output, we model distinct translation pathways as agents operating over a shared multilingual backbone. Inter-agent divergence is treated not as error but as an interpretable behavioral signal. We conduct an empirical study on Turkish--Syrian Arabic translation using three agents: (1) zero-shot direct translation, (2) dialect-stabilized translation via lightweight fine-tuning, and (3) pivot translation through English. Evaluation is performed on 5,000 dialogue sentences, while stabilization is trained on 5,000 additional Turkish--Syrian sentence pairs drawn from television dialogue and MADAR-Turk resources. Rather than optimizing for conventional performance metrics, we quantify structured behavioral displacement using dialect marker frequency, lexical proximity to standardized Arabic, and structural variance. Lightweight stabilization nearly doubles dialect marker usage, increasing it from 0.2266 to 0.4988, while significantly reducing structural instability. Pivot mediation introduces normalization pressure and measurable compression effects, whereas zero-shot translation exhibits the highest decision variance. We argue that translation divergence across agents reveals latent decision flexibility within multilingual models and we provide a principled interpretability framework for low-resource dialect generation.

title: Mitigating Statistical Non-Independence in Distributed Facial Recognition Systems through Personalized Federated Learning and Feature Alignment Techniques
authors: Thenmozhi R, M. Santhalakshmi, M. Shanthakumar
abstract: Statistical non-independence poses a critical challenge in federated learning systems for facial recognition, where distributed client data exhibits inherent correlations that violate fundamental independence assumptions. This paper proposes a novel framework combining personalized federated learning (PFL) with adaptive feature alignment techniques to mitigate these statistical dependencies. Our method introduces a two-stage approach: (1) local personalization that captures client-specific data distributions through adaptive model parameters, and (2) cross-client feature alignment that normalizes learned representations to a common latent space, reducing inter-client correlations. We introduce two novel evaluation metrics—Feature Independence Score (FIS) and Cross-Client Alignment Quality (CCAQ)—specifically designed to quantify statistical non-independence and feature homogeneity in distributed systems. Comprehensive experiments on VGGFace2 and MS-Celeb-1M datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves 95.7% accuracy on the proposed framework, surpassing standard federated learning by 2.3 percentage points while reducing feature dependency by 0.892 on the FIS metric. Results validate that addressing statistical non-independence significantly improves model convergence and generalization in privacy-preserving facial recognition systems.

We introduce two novel evaluation metrics—Feature Independence Score (FIS) and Cross-Client Alignment Quality (CCAQ)—specifically designed to quantify statistical non-independence and feature homogeneity in distributed systems. Comprehensive experiments on VGGFace2 and MS-Celeb-1M datasets demonstrate that our approach achieves 95.7% accuracy on the proposed framework, surpassing standard federated learning by 2.3 percentage points while reducing feature dependency by 0.892 on the FIS metric. Results validate that addressing statistical non-independence significantly improves model convergence and generalization in privacy-preserving facial recognition systems.

title: An Adaptive Personalized Federated Learning Framework for Secure and Robust Pregnancy Risk Prediction
abstract: Pregnancy-related complications continue to be an important concern in maternal healthcare, particularly in situations where early identification of high-risk pregnancies can support timely medical intervention. Machine learning has shown promising results in predicting maternal health risks from physiological and clinical parameters. However, most conventional machine-learning approaches depend on centralized healthcare datasets, requiring sensitive patient information to be transferred to a common location. Such centralized data management can introduce concerns related to privacy, security, data ownership, regulatory compliance, and institutional data-sharing policies.Federated Learning (FL) offers an alternative by allowing healthcare institutions to collaboratively train a machine-learning model while keeping patient records within their respective institutions. However, healthcare data rarely follow identical distributions across hospitals. Differences in patient demographics, geographical conditions, disease prevalence, clinical practices, and available healthcare facilities can lead to highly non-independent and identically distributed (non-IID) data. Under such conditions, a single global model may not provide equally effective predictions for all participating institutions.To address this limitation, this study proposes an Adaptive Personalized Federated Learning (APFL) framework for privacy-preserving pregnancy risk prediction. The proposed framework combines personalized local models, adaptive client aggregation, differential privacy, and secure aggregation. Participating healthcare institutions act as decentralized clients and train the prediction model using locally available pregnancy-related data. Instead of sharing patient records, protected model updates are transmitted to a coordinating server. The server adaptively combines these updates, while personalized model components allow individual institutions to retain knowledge specific to their local patient population.The proposed framework will be evaluated using accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC). Additional evaluation will consider communication overhead and privacy-related performance. The study aims to demonstrate that adaptive personalization can improve the robustness of federated pregnancy-risk prediction when healthcare data are heterogeneous, while simultaneously reducing the exposure of sensitive patient information. The proposed framework can provide a foundation for developing scalable and trustworthy artificial intelligence solutions for decentralized maternal healthcare. Keywords: Federated Learning, Pregnancy Risk Prediction, Maternal Healthcare, Non-IID Data, Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning

title: Feedback-Driven Self-Consistency Validation (FSCV)
abstract: This paper introduces Feedback-Driven Self-Consistency Validation (FSCV), a novel self-consistency validation technique designed to enhance the reliability and accuracy of machine learning models. The core principle of FSCV leverages continuous feedback loops to identify and mitigate discrepancies in model outputs, thereby fostering a more robust and dependable system. We present a framework for automated parameter adjustment based on these discrepancies, ensuring consistent and reliable predictions across a range of inputs. The research explores the practical application of FSCV in [mention specific application area, e.g., text summarization, image recognition], demonstrating its potential to significantly improve model performance. We address challenges related to parameter tuning and provide a detailed implementation of the FSCV algorithm.

title: Title: Fractal Geometry with Adaptive Scale for Machine Learning
abstract: Fractal geometry, characterized by self-repeating patterns at different scales, offers a powerful tool for modeling complex data and enhancing machine learning performance. This paper explores the application of adaptive scale in fractal geometry for improving generalization capabilities. We propose a novel algorithm that dynamically adjusts the scale of fractal elements during the training process, leveraging a scale-aware representation learning mechanism. This approach addresses a critical challenge in deep learning – the need for robust generalization – by incorporating adaptive scale. The study demonstrates that this method significantly improves the performance of machine learning models on a range of datasets, showcasing the benefits of this novel approach.

title: Time-Dependent Topological Structures
abstract: This paper investigates the application of time-dependent topological structures to the design of quantum circuits, aiming to enhance the reliability of quantum computation. Traditional quantum circuit design relies on static topologies, limiting design flexibility and robustness. We propose a novel approach leveraging time-dependent topological structures to construct quantum circuits with inherent stability. The core mechanism involves the generation of a dynamically evolving topological network, allowing for the detection and mitigation of potential instability through iterative refinement. The paper presents preliminary results demonstrating the effectiveness of this approach in stabilizing quantum circuits, offering a promising pathway towards more robust and reliable quantum devices. This research addresses a critical challenge in quantum computing – ensuring circuit stability – by introducing a fundamentally new topological design paradigm.

title: Quantum Information Topology
abstract: Quantum information, the fundamental building block of modern computation, possesses unique topological properties that profoundly impact its stability and robustness. This research delves into a novel mathematical framework, Quantum Information Topology, to better understand and quantify these topological aspects. We propose a new conceptualization of entanglement as a geometric entity, leveraging concepts from topology and geometry to derive rigorous predictions about the behavior of quantum systems. This framework seeks to provide a more comprehensive and predictive model for the evolution of quantum information, moving beyond traditional approaches that often fall short in capturing these intricate relationships. The core claim is that this framework will offer a deeper understanding of the topology of quantum information and its influence on system stability.

title: Bayesian Neural Network Resonance (BNNR)
abstract: This paper introduces Bayesian Neural Network Resonance (BNNR), a novel architecture for neural networks designed to enhance learning and generalization through a dynamically adjusted feedback loop. We propose a mechanism that incorporates a resonance effect, iteratively refining network weights based on the network's output. This approach mitigates the vanishing gradient problem and promotes stable learning, leading to improved performance on a diverse range of datasets. We detail the core architecture, the feedback loop implementation, and experimental results demonstrating the effectiveness of BNRR compared to existing methods. The paper concludes with a discussion of the potential applications of BNRR in various machine learning domains.
